gist: Brent Johnson explains the dollar index breakout above 102 under a hawkish Fed chair Warsh, argues Fed and Treasury are fusing for a US-China great-power contest (including a latent remarking of $42/oz gold certificates worth ~$1 trillion), and sees the late-1940s Cold War, not the 1970s, as the analog. The trading segment flags a CAD put, 5.35% 10-year yields, thin equity breadth and crowded oil and natgas positioning.

themes.theme: Dollar breakout and the milkshake framework

insights.claim: The dollar index closed above 102 on Oct 8 2026, breaking out despite summer consensus that Warsh-led Fed would cut and weaken the dollar; Warsh instead raised rates to establish credibility.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Consensus dollar-bear positioning was caught offside by a hawkish new Fed chair.

insights.claim: Johnson gives four drivers of dollar strength: higher Fed rates, no attractive alternative (Europe war and no fiscal union, Japan problems, China closed market amid trade war), structural global dollar liabilities, and an AI-growth narrative lifting real rates.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Owning dollars is the first step before choosing T-bills, equities or real estate; the bid is structural, not just rate-driven.
insights.quote: where else are you going to go, right?

insights.claim: Positioning, sentiment and momentum in the euro and gold have washed out and gold just had a golden cross (50-day through 100-day), so a short-term dollar pullback with a euro and gold bounce is plausible; if the dollar instead keeps rising, it will start to break things.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Tactical window for a dollar pullback, but a disorderly further spike is a systemic risk.

insights.claim: The milkshake theory's call of a global sovereign debt crisis driving the dollar back to all-time highs (~116) was wrong on timing because authorities kicked the can in 2020 and 2022, but the direction of asset moves it predicted held; in an endgame the dollar is more likely to spike than fall.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Framework still guides allocation even though the crisis catalyst has been deferred.
insights.quote: the direction that the I said the assets would travel as a result of that sovereign debt crisis has been correct

insights.claim: The US can absorb more pain than others: as the big stack at the poker table, higher rates, stock drawdowns or energy shocks hurt weaker players more, and the US happily takes hits while taking the left tail (becoming the small stack) off the table.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Relative-pain framing supports owning USD assets over foreign ones in a global rate shock.

insights.claim: Carry-style expression: owning USD T-bills versus Canadian dollars earns about an extra percent of yield while CAD weakens, which is how the US sucks in global capital; Johnson called the long UST / short Canada trade not a horrible one.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Rate differentials plus higher-beta foreign rate stress favor long USD / short CAD.

insights.claim: If DXY reaches 110, Johnson expects gold to fall to roughly $3,700 from about $4,100, and a break of current support could mean another 10% drop; yet he bought gold for a client the day before and sees this as the area to start nibbling, expecting a sizable move in coming weeks.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Gold downside scenario is tied to dollar strength; accumulation zone near $4,000 with buying of any dip to $3,700.

insights.claim: US sovereign gold (about 8,000 tons) is carried on Fed gold certificates at $42/oz; remarking to market (~$4,100) would have the Fed credit Treasury's account with roughly $1 trillion in an afternoon, requiring Treasury and Fed to cooperate.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: A latent, fast fiscal-liquidity tool that is a monetary-fiscal merger mechanism; relevant to gold as a policy backstop.

insights.claim: Johnson concedes the gold remarking is an accounting trick that adds money supply and dilutes each dollar, akin to the 1930s confiscate-and-revalue; he does not expect it soon because a rising dollar means no need to restore confidence, and Judy Shelton's Treasury advisory role is not evidence of intent.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Treat revaluation as an insurance option, not a near-term catalyst; a falling dollar and confidence loss would be the trigger.

insights.claim: Roughly 6,000 tons of foreign gold held at the New York Fed could be taken into US custody in an extreme scenario, with token credits to depositors; Erik Townsend floated a gold-backed stablecoin on US reserves as an extension, which Johnson does not expect but cannot rule out.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Tail-risk of sovereign gold being weaponized or tokenized; supports tail-hedge demand for physical gold outside US custody.

insights.claim: Johnson argues the Fed has 'a lot more bullets than you can possibly imagine' and he has heard 'Fed is out of bullets' for 25 of his 26 years in markets.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Don't bet on policy exhaustion; authorities have many unconventional tools to extend the cycle.
insights.quote: for 25 of the 26 years I've been hearing that the Fed is out of bullets

insights.claim: Johnson contends Fed independence is really autonomy (it needs a congressional charter and testifies twice a year), and in a great-power competition the sovereign will demand a united front, pushing the Fed and Treasury toward coordinated policy.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Expect fiscal-dominance style coordination: yield-curve, buyback and liquidity policy aligned with executive goals.

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent has been entering traditionally monetary territory (Treasury buybacks, swap lines) over 18 months, and when asked how the new Fed chair would react to increased buybacks he said 'we will work together' rather than staying in lanes.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Buybacks and swap lines are now Treasury tools, signalling blurred fiscal-monetary boundaries.

insights.claim: Historical precedent shows Fed and Treasury often at odds: the 1950s Treasury-Fed Accord, and in 2022 Powell raised rates while Yellen drew down the TGA and reverse repo, injecting liquidity against the Fed's tightening.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Counterbalancing TGA/RRP flows can offset Fed tightening; track them when judging liquidity.

insights.claim: Stablecoins let Treasury distribute debt, raise cash and make payments without the banking system, eroding the Fed's historic leverage as the dollar's distribution arm; Johnson says this shifts power toward Treasury over 5-10 years.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth is a structural bid for T-bills and a fiscal-dominance enabler.

insights.claim: Erik Townsend notes Bessent is participating in wartime policy design, including economic sanctions against Iran, beyond Treasury's traditional scope.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Treasury is acting as a geopolitical instrument, raising sanctions and energy-policy risk.

themes.theme: US rates, bond selloff and passive flows

insights.claim: Johnson attributes higher US yields to reduced enthusiasm for buying Treasuries amid Trump policy uncertainty (not wholesale rejection), AI-driven growth requiring more term premium, and passive/machine selling of bonds as prices fall.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Passive-flow dislocations in sovereign bonds could produce fast, non-fundamental yield spikes.

insights.claim: Johnson's concern is not US rates themselves but knock-on effects abroad; rates in Europe, South America and Asia are rising severely too, and a global rate shock hurts weaker sovereigns more.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Rising global yields point to relative stress outside the US and support the dollar.

insights.claim: 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.35% and the 30-year nearly 5.8% while equities remain near highs, a two-regime divergence where only 20% of stocks were above their 50-day moving average earlier in the week.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices trading desk)
insights.so_what: Bond selloff and poor breadth are a warning that equities may be forced to reprice higher hurdle rates.

themes.theme: Great power competition, Cold War analog and AI

insights.claim: Johnson says the better analog is the late 1940s-50s Cold War (high WWII debt, long contest with a rival), now with China, rather than the 1970s inflation era; he expects a 30-40 year swing away from globalization.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Structural deglobalization and a debt-laden rivalry favor strategic assets and policy coordination over a 1970s inflation playbook.

insights.claim: Johnson draws a Rome parallel: the late Roman Republic (120-60 BC) had draining foreign wars, inequality and political infighting, and what followed was Empire under a strongman, not collapse; he sees empire consolidation as more likely for the US than decline.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Anticipate centralization of executive power rather than US decline when positioning long-term.

insights.claim: Countries will be forced to choose sides in the US-China contest and winning the power competition requires winning AI; China's electricity output gives it an advantage, and chips and energy are being weaponized (e.g., Rubio in Iceland, Venezuela action).
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Energy and chips policy are geopolitical levers; US energy buildout is decisive for AI leadership.

insights.claim: Chinese open-source AI models run on-premise are cited as only 3-6 months behind frontier labs and could be air-gapped from US cloud providers; a host warns this could crash AI-linked private credit if enterprises abandon OpenAI and Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Commoditization risk to frontier AI revenue and the private credit financing behind it.

insights.claim: Johnson calls the open-source threat a real concern he neither fully agrees nor disagrees with, adding that China being right behind the frontier may not matter commercially.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Taking China's AI parity seriously tempers assumptions of US AI winner-take-all.
insights.quote: if they're just either right there or right behind it, does it really matter?

insights.claim: Johnson's base case is that AI is a net positive step-change, with short-term unemployment likely addressed via universal basic income or expanded welfare to avoid unrest.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Expect fiscal expansion and transfers as policy response to AI job displacement.

themes.theme: Market positioning and tactical trades (MacroVoices desk)

insights.claim: Patrick proposes buying the 70 put on CAD futures (Nov 6 2026 expiry) at 22 pips, with CAD near 70.37 cents and implied vol under 5%, to express Johnson's USD thesis; target 69 cents yields roughly 3.5x return on premium and risk is limited to premium.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices trading desk)
insights.so_what: Cheap-vol, defined-risk way to express long USD vs CAD.

insights.claim: Equity indices hold highs through only Nvidia and Microsoft leadership ('MAG 2'), the Russell and equal-weight S&P are in downtrends, and systematic triggers near S&P 7700 (about 2.5% below highs) could unleash up to $85 billion of selling.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices trading desk)
insights.so_what: Thin breadth plus a nearby systematic-selling threshold makes index downside convex.

insights.claim: Euro has broken support lines and could fall toward 110 or 108 as Europe is a net energy importer vulnerable to supply disruption, while the dollar breakout shows no immediate catalyst to reverse.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices trading desk)
insights.so_what: Euro weakness is energy-linked and supports the dollar trend.

insights.claim: Crude is near $93 with Hormuz and Oman lane attack concerns, thin inventories and speculative gross shorts at a five-year extreme; the $10 front-month reversal contrasts with Jan and Mar contracts still making new highs.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices trading desk)
insights.so_what: Oil breakout above $100 would raise rates and could break equities; short-covering risk is high.

insights.claim: Gold is under pressure from rising real rates and dollar funding stress; precious-metals CoT positioning (silver, platinum) sits near 0 percentile on one-year lookback, and a break below $4,000 would be a corrective long-term buying opportunity, not an imminent bullish turn.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices trading desk)
insights.so_what: Macro regime is a headwind for gold near term, though positioning is washed out.

insights.claim: Natural gas gross short positioning is at a record with 0 percentile readings across 1-, 3- and 5-year lookbacks, and early-season cold forecasts create short-squeeze risk.
insights.speaker: Patrick (MacroVoices trading desk)
insights.so_what: Crowded shorts and weather catalyst set up a potential squeeze rally.
